paper_title: SkillSeek: Revisiting Agent Skill Retrieval at Marketplace Scale

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Anthropic's Agent Skills package reusable procedural know-how for an LLM agent into SKILL.md directories, and open-source aggregations have grown past 230,000 skills, making selection rather than authoring the bottleneck. The standing answer in the literature outsources selection to the agent itself: an LLM-mediated retrieval loop that rewrites queries and refines candidates inside the agent's decision loop, paying LLM tokens on every task. We present SkillSeek, an open-source two-stage skill retriever built from the standard IR recipe (a BGE-base bi-encoder feeding a small cross-encoder, exposed over MCP). Across a $4 \times 11$ grid of pool, backbone, and method on the 89-task SkillsBench benchmark, SkillSeek reaches observed parity with the LLM-mediated loop of Liu et al. at essentially no extra cost: plain bm25 alone records a pass rate at or above their refined loop on three of four settings, and a small cross-encoder covers the remaining difference on the fourth. A first-stage recall ceiling explains the pattern, and total per-trial spend drops from USD 51.30 to USD 27.54 (within fifty cents of the no-skill baseline). Under the SkillsBench tasks and OpenHands harness we tested, this positions the standard IR recipe as a strong default for agent-skill retrieval, with LLM-mediated alternatives a natural fit for cases where deterministic methods fall short.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: At deployment time, an LLM can be augmented with task-specific procedural knowledge through several mechanisms: function calling,1 MCP servers,2 persistent project instructions like *Accepted at AACL-IJCNLP 2026. This is the authors preprint version. 1https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/buildwith-claude/tool-use 2https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ CLAUDE.md,3 RAG,4 and sub-agents.5 Anthropics Agent Skills extend this toolkit with distinctive mechanism: each skill is SKILL.md directory that loads progressively (a roughly 30-token metadata entry at startup, full body when judged relevant, bundled scripts and resources on demand), leaving the agent harness to decide which skills to surface per task (Xu and Yan, 2026).6 This selection problem becomes acute at scale. Open-source aggregations of public skills have grown rapidly: 47,150 (Li et al., 2026), 55,315 (Gao et al., 2026), over 118,000 (Chen et al., 2026), and 238,180 across major distribution platforms in the most recent crawl (Holzbauer et al., 2026). natural first idea is to load the entire pool into the agents context: modern LLMs have large enough context windows to fit the full pool. But even at modest size (192 skills), loading every skill into the agents context already leaves pass rate at the no-skill baseline while inflating token cost by 59% (Appendix F). Loading curated subset is not free fix either: the lift from adding skills is non-monotonic (Li et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026) (SkillsBench), with one relevant skill lifting the agent by +17.8%, twoto-three by +18.6%, but four or more regressing to +5.9%. retriever therefore has to be precise about which skills to load, not just to surface any reasonable candidate. The standing answer in the literature is to outsource selection to the agent itself. Liu et al. (2026b) pair BM25 with dense embedding via reciprocal-rank fusion over 34,000-skill marketplace pool, and let the agent iteratively rewrite the query, explore retrieved candidates, and synthe3https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory 4https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/buildwith-claude/contextual-retrieval 5https://docs.claude.com/en/api/agentsdk/subagents 6https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/ equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agentskills 1 Figure 1: deterministic two-stage retriever reaches observed parity with an LLM-mediated retrieval loop at pytest verifier, zero in-loop LLM cost. Left: the task-solving loop (task which returns graded reward in [0, 1]). Right: two methods that occupy the retrieval step, SkillSeek (top, bi-encoder + cross-encoder over MCP) and Liu et al. (2026b)s liu_refined (bottom, LLM agent refinement loop), with cost-vs-pass-rate Pareto plots on both pools. skill-retrieval module agent size them into task-specific refined skill inside its own decision loop. The design has real strengths. On Terminal-Bench 2.0 tensor-parallelism case they document, the agent first retrieves two partially relevant skills (torch-tensor-parallel and pytorch-research). It then composes new skill that merges weight-sharding from the first with custom autograd.Function patterns from the second, synthesis that no single skill provides on its own and that static retriever cannot produce. When the right skills exist in the pool but no single one suffices, the LLM-mediated loop delivers something static retriever cannot. How often this advantage fires in practice is an empirical question. On the SkillsBench 89task benchmark, plain bm25 already records pass rate at or above Liu et al. (2026b)s refined loop on three of four (pool, backbone) settings, and SkillSeek (a bi-encoder + small cross-encoder) covers the remaining difference on the fourth (34K pool with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B; 4.2). But accuracy parity does not extend to cost. Liu et al. (2026b)s loop pays LLM tokens on every task, including the settings where its synthesis advantage is not needed  (Table 6)  : liu_hybrid runs agentic retrieval inside the task agents loop, inflating that loop by 44% ($39.43 vs. $27.41 for no skills); liu_refined adds separate refinement agent before the task agent, totaling $51.30 for +9.0% over no skills. SkillSeek reaches observed parity with liu_refined at essentially no extra cost. On the headline 34K / Qwen3.5 setting its Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B variant records the same 0.442 pass rate as liu_refined, while its default bge-reranker-v2-m3 variant lifts pass rate by +5.7% over no skills against liu_refineds +9.0%. Both variants run on CPU with zero LLM tokens and leave the agents spend within fifty cents of the no-skill floor ($27.54 vs. $27.41). Contribution. We present SkillSeek, an opensource two-stage skill retriever (BGE-base biencoder feeding small cross-encoder, exposed over MCP) implementing the standard IR recipe. 11 grid Our contribution is empirical: across 4 of pool, backbone, and method, the deterministic recipe reaches agent pass-rate comparable to LLMmediated retrieval, at zero in-loop LLM cost. Under the SkillsBench tasks and OpenHands harness we tested, this positions the standard IR recipe as strong default starting point for agent-skill retrieval, with LLM-mediated alternatives natural fit for cases where the deterministic recipe falls short. We open-source SkillSeek, including the scripts that regenerate every number in this paper, at https: //github.com/guanqun-yang/SkillSeek.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agent Skills. Li et al. (2026) contribute SkillsBench, the 89-task benchmark we evaluate on, and report that curated SKILL.md bundles (Xu and Yan, 2026) add +16.2% on average across 7 model+harness configurations while bundles of 4 or more skills regress to +5.9%. Han et al. (2026) find similar per-skill variance: 39 of 49 public SWE skills yield zero pass-rate change; only 7 produce meaningful gains on domain-specific tasks. Skill Selection and Retrieval. Liu et al. (2026b) run the closest analogue: agentic-hybrid retrieval over 34,000-skill marketplace pool, pairing BM25 with Qwen3-Embedding-4B and delegating second-stage filtering to the agent, with optional query-specific refinement. They report passrate degradation from curated to marketplace-scale conditions (Claude Opus 4.6 drops from 51.2% with curated skills to 40.1% when retrieving from the 34K pool). Their query-specific refinement recovers most of this loss (Claude Opus 4.6 climbs to 48.2%) but pays an LLM-mediated exploration pass per task. SkillSeek provides the deterministicretrieval point of comparison alongside Liu et al. (2026b)s LLM-mediated loop, sharing sparseplus-dense first stage but diverging at the reranker. Contemporaneous with this work, Zheng et al. (2026) study the same routing problem on SkillsBench-derived pool of approximately 80K skills.7 They report that hiding the skill body costs 37 to 44 points of routing accuracy, and present 1.2 body-aware retrieve-and-rerank pipeline reaching 74.0% Hit@1. Two differences separate their setting from ours: they fine-tune their own encoder and reranker, where our recipe is training-free and off-the-shelf, and they report neither comparison against an LLM-mediated retrieval loop nor any token or monetary cost, which is the axis our contribution turns on. Their body-isdecisive finding and our indexing ablation (4.3), where appending the raw skill body lowers downstream pass rate by 3.2%, measure different quantities: routing accuracy asks whether the gold skill is ranked first, and agent pass rate asks whether the surfaced skill helps the agent finish the task. Our helpfulness-gap diagnostic (4.4) shows these two can move in opposite directions. 7Posted 23 March 2026, within the three-month window of the ACL Policies for Review and Citation at our 25 May submission date. We discuss it here as concurrent work. Creating and Securing the Skill Pool. parallel line of work builds and secures the pool. On the authoring side, recent work compresses skill text by 48%/39% (description/body) (Gao et al., 2026), tunes skill bundles as bi-objective search over (pass rate, cost) (Gong et al., 2026), compiles skills as code for +15.3% task completion (Chen et al., 2026), and mines skills automatically with 71.1% novelty against existing libraries (Shen et al., 2026). On the trust side, guidance-injection attacks reach 16% to 64% trial success and evade 94% of scanners (Liu et al., 2026a), 121 marketplace skills point to abandoned, claimable repositories (Holzbauer et al., 2026), and pre-load risk scoring reaches 0.800 F1 at six tenths of US cent per skill (Hou and Yang, 2026), natural composition with SkillSeeks retrieval (J).

sections.title: 3 SkillSeek
sections.content: SkillSeek is deterministic two-stage retriever that sits between the agent and the skill pool. We expose it as an MCP server so that any harness that already supports MCP (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenHands, and others) can adopt it without sourcelevel changes. Figure 1 depicts the deployment. 3.1 Two-Stage Retriever At lookup time the agent submits naturallanguage query, and SkillSeek runs two stages. The first stage scores the query against every indexed skill with the BGE-base bi-encoder (110 parameters, 768-dim embeddings) and returns the top-20 candidates by cosine similarity. The second stage reranks the 20 candidate (query, skill) pairs jointly with the bge-reranker-v2-m3 cross-encoder (568 parameters) and returns the top-5 by cross-encoder score. two secondaries); The indexed text for each skill is its name and description, appended with four-tag ToolREX v3 structured profile (file-type, primary opthe SKILL.md body eration, is not indexed and is fetched only on demand. Names and descriptions alone often miss the filetype and operation surface forms that the crossencoder uses, while appending the raw body adds noise; the Tool-REX profile is generated offline by an LLM following Lu et al. (2025), and we ablate this choice against name+description and name+description+body in Table 2. For example, the pdf-excel-diff skill is indexed as the concatenation shown in Listing 1: the four tags (pdf, compare, excel, xlsx) restore exactly the surface forms the cross-encoder needs. Listing 1: Indexed text for the pdf-excel-diff skill under Tool-REX v3 expansion (name, description, fourtag profile). pdf - excel - diff Compare PDF document against an Excel spreadsheet , flagging cells whose values differ . pdf , compare , excel , xlsx 1 2 3 For the analysis in 4.4 we additionally swap the cross-encoder for Qwen3-Reranker variants and commercial-API rerankers; only the stage-2 model changes, while the bi-encoder, the indexing, and the top-k are held fixed. 3.2 MCP Server Interface SkillSeek exposes three tools to the agent over MCP. skill_lookup(query, k) returns the top-k candidates as name: description lines; skill_ load(name) returns the full SKILL.md body for named skill; skill_list() returns every skill name and description. server-side X-SkillMethod HTTP header lets the experimental driver override which retriever skill_lookup runs without changing the agents tool schema, keeping all per-condition runs in 4 directly comparable across conditions. 3.3 Driver and Harness The MCP server is harness-agnostic by construction. For the experiments in this paper we drive the OpenHands SDK directly: its in-process Python agent loop lets our driver capture per-turn events, and its native MCP support lets us inject mcp_ config when swapping retrieval backends between conditions. discussion against alternative harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Terminus-2) is in Appendix B.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Setup Skill Pools. We evaluated on two pools of contrasting size and curation. The 192-skill curated pool is the SkillsBench corpus (Li et al., 2026): 89 deterministically-verified tasks paired with 233 raw SKILL.md files that deduplicate to 192 unique skill names.8 The 34K marketplace pool is the open 8A note on the related counts that appear in this paper: 89 is the full SkillsBench task set we use throughout; 233 is the total number of SKILL.md files across the 89 tasks environment/skills/ directories (approximately 2.6 skills collection from Liu et al. (2026b), harvested from public skill hubs and filtered by permissive licenses and content quality. The first pool measures the quality ceiling of retrieval when every relevant skill is in the catalog; the second measures effectiveness when the agent must find the right skill among many irrelevant ones. Agent Backbones. The primary backbone is Qwen3.5-397B-A17B; the secondary backbone is MiniMax-M2.7, weaker by approximately 99 CodeArena points and noisier in our trials.9 Both are served through OpenRouter. Table 9 in the Appendix lists the canonical identifier for every model used in this paper. Agent Harness. We used the OpenHands SDK as the agent harness: it is open-source, modelagnostic, scriptable from Python, and ships native MCP and skill-loading modules, which our experimental driver depends on for swapping retrieval backends without changing the agents tool schema. The full comparison against alternative harnesses is in Appendix B. Methods. Each setting of Table 1 evaluates one retrieval method paired with fixed agent backbone over the 89 SkillsBench tasks. All methods serve the agents skill_lookup tool with the top-5 skills they select from their respective pool, except liu_refined which serves the 1 to 3 skills its refinement step selects. We compared four families: Reference: none mounts no skills. Classical IR: bm25 alone. OSS retriever (ours): BGE-base bi-encoder over the top-20 candidates, followed by stage-2 reranker (568 M-parameter bgereranker-v2-m3 or Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B); the analysis in 4.4 additionally swaps in Qwen3-Reranker-4B/8B and commercial-API rerankers (Voyage rerank-2.5, rerank-2.5-lite). two variants. liu_hybrid runs their agentic retrieval (BM25 fused with Qwen3-Embedding-4B via reciprocal-rank fusion over top-60) inside the Baseline (Liu et al. We reimplement both inside our driver (Appendix D). The text indexed by the OSS retriever family is the skills name and description appended with four-tag Tool-REX v3 structured profile (file-type, primary operation, two secondaries), generated offline by an LLM following Lu et al. (2025); see Appendix for the exact prompt and comparison against earlier iterations. Evaluation Protocol. Each trial is single agent run capped at 30 turns and 600 seconds of wallclock. Every SkillsBench task ships with deterministic pytest verifier. The verifier is deterministic but not binary: tasks assertions are scored as group, so trial receives graded reward in [0, 1] equal to the fraction of the tasks checks that pass, and partial credit is common (for example, enterprise-information-search scores 0.200 and weighted-gdp-calc scores 0.593 on single trial). We report the agent pass rate: the mean graded reward over the 89 tasks, with missing trials counted as 0.10 Table 1 reports this pass rate for every setting of the main grid; first-stage retrieval recall (R@5) is reported separately in 4.4  (Table 5)  . Full harness, MCP server, and trial-budget details are in Appendix C. 4.2 Main Results Table 1 reports the main results: agent pass rate 11 grid of (pool, backbone) pairs across the 4 and retrieval methods. These are observed differences on single trial per cell, and we do not claim any of them as resolved advantage in either direction (see Limitations). Lightweight Rerankers Win on Curated Pools; Heavier Rerankers and LLM Refinement Win on Marketplace Pools. Which method wins changes with the size of the pool. On the small curated pool, the simplest methods are best: bm25 leads on MiniMax-M2.7, and our roughly 0.5 Bparameter cross-encoder bge-reranker-v2-m3 leads on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. On the large marketplace pool, the heavier methods catch up: Qwen3Reranker-0.6B (0.442) ties liu_refined (0.442) on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. The same trend shows up if we track each method across pools: going from the 192 pool to the 34K pool on Qwen3.5-397BA17B, the two lighter methods lose ground (bgereranker-v2-m3 drops 7.1%, liu_hybrid drops 5.3%), while the two heavier methods improve (Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B rises 1.2%, liu_refined rises 4.5%). (iii) Top-3 captures essentially all the gain over rank-1: beyond = 3, additional candidates buy nothing. 4.4 Analysis We now examine three questions raised by the main result: (i) what mechanism explains why lightweight rerankers suffice on curated pools but heavier ones help on marketplace pools; (ii) Figure 2: Reranker scaling and OSS-vs-commercial. 34K pool with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. (a) Pass rate plateaus within the Qwen3-Reranker family at the 0.6B size; Qwen3-Reranker-8B narrowly beats Voyage rerank-2.5 by +1.5%. (b) The helpfulness gap (passrate conditional on the gold skill being retrieved minus pass-rate conditional on miss) explains why: Voyage rerank-2.5 is the only reranker with negative helpfulness gap, meaning its retrievals do not translate into agent success. does scaling the reranker further close the gap to LLM-mediated refinement; and (iii) how do opensource rerankers compare with commercial-API rerankers? First-Stage Recall Ceiling Explains Why Lightweight Rerankers Suffice on Curated Pools. We propose that the split follows from single mechanism: cross-encoder capacity helps proportionally to how much relevant-document recall remains beyond stage-1. Table 5 operationalizes the claim. On the 192 pool, bm25 alone reaches R@5 = 0.546 and the BGE-base bi-encoder matches it; the bge-reranker-v2-m3 cross-encoder adds only +3.5%. Stage-1 recall is at or near ceiling: the pool was hand-built to contain the right skill, lexical metadata-matching is already sufficient, and adding capacity past bge-reranker-v2-m3 cannot lift top-1 precision. On the 34K pool, the same comparison shows bm25 at 0.391 and BGEbase at 0.379, far from ceiling, and the reranker adds +5.4%, growing to +9.9% once Tool-REX v3 further restructures the index. This pattern is consistent with prior work. Rosa et al. (2022) report that monoT5 capacity helps far more outof-domain than in-domain (+0.107 nDCG@10 vs. +0.042 MRR over the same 60 to 3 sweep). Li 7 et al. (2024) confirm the reverse direction: queryexpansion makes strong cross-encoders worse on clean test sets. Together these predict exactly what we observe: low-capacity rerankers suffice when the right skill is already at the top of the candidate list, while high-capacity rerankers (and LLM refinement) only help when the right skill sits lower in the list and needs to be promoted. Scaling Rerankers Plateaus near 0.6 B, and Open-Source Rerankers Beat the Commercial Alternatives We Tested. Figure 2(a) reports pass rates for six rerankers on the 34K pool with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. Within the Qwen3Reranker family, scaling is essentially flat: 0.6B reaches 0.442, 4B drops to 0.430 (a non-monotone dip), and 8B recovers to 0.450, marginal +0.7% gain over 0.6B from 13 parameter increase. The strongest single-reranker configuration only matches liu_refined (0.442), consistent with the recall ceiling above bounding what any stage-2 reranker can achieve at this corpus scale. Against the commercial alternative, Qwen3-Reranker-8B (0.450) narrowly beats Voyage rerank-2.5 (0.435) by +1.5%, with 13 wins, 67 ties, and 9 losses on the 89-task paired comparison. To explain why Voyage rerank-2.5 underperforms despite having the highest top-5 recall, we define diagnostic we call the helpfulness gap. For retriever m, partition the 89 tasks into hit set Gm (where ms top-5 contains curated gold skill) and miss set Gm (where it does not); the helpfulness gap is = Et Gm[passt] Et Gm[passt]. positive gap means retrieving the gold helps the agent; negative gap means it actively hurts. Figure 2(b) shows Voyage rerank-2.5 with the highest top-5 recall (72.2%) but negative help0.025): retrieving Voyages fulness gap ( = notion of the gold skill is slightly worse for the agent than missing it. Qwen3-Reranker-8B sits at the top ( = +0.149); bge-reranker-v2-m3 is near zero ( = +0.012). The mechanism is that our agent commits to the rank-1 candidate on roughly 65% of tasks, so what matters is the rank-1 skill being task-useful, not whether the gold is somewhere in top-5 (the AgentSkills specification leaves ranking versus browsing up to the host harness (Xu and Yan, 2026)). Difficulty easy medium hard 6 52 26 none rerank lift 0.254 0.324 0. 0.306 +5.2% 0.378 +5.4% 0.274 +8.0% Table 8: Per-difficulty lift. Rerank-vs-none lift on the 34K pool with MiniMax-M2.7; difficulty labels come from task.toml, with 3 of 89 tasks unlabeled. its rank-1 over-promotes semantically-similar nongold skills; the same explains the Qwen3-Reranker4B dip in panel (a). Per-Task Wins and Losses. Table 7 reports the largest per-task deltas of rerank vs. none on the 34K pool with MiniMax-M2.7. Two patterns dominate. The largest positive lifts (+0.89 to +1.00) occur where the gold skills name and description match the agents query closely; examples include flood-risk-analysis and gravitational-wave-detection. The largest negative lifts (-0.50 to -0.80) occur where another pool skill is near-twin in description and the crossencoder picks the wrong one, as on paralleltfidf-search and adaptive-cruise-control. The losses are not coverage failures (the gold is in the pool); they are ranking failures driven by lexical near-twins that the cross-encoder lacks verifieraware signal to disambiguate. Per-Difficulty Stratification. Table 8 stratifies the rerank-vs-none lift by SkillsBench difficulty. The lift is largest on hard tasks (+8.0%), modest on medium tasks (+5.4%), and similar on easy tasks (+5.2%). The hard-task gain is the cleanest signal: hard tasks have the lowest no-retrieval baseline (0.194) and therefore the most headroom that retrieval can convert into pass rate, consistent with the recall-ceiling argument above. tives natural fit where it falls short. Cost Breakdown. Table 6 decomposes the total per-trial token cost into retrieval-side component and main-agent-loop component on the 34K pool with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. SkillSeek pays nothing on the retrieval side: the bi-encoder and cross-encoder run on CPU at approximately 1.1 median per skill_lookup call (1.9 at p95), and the agents own spend stays within fifty cents of the no-skill baseline ($27.54 vs. $27.41). liu_hybrid keeps the retrieval LLM-cost at zero but pays 44% surcharge on the agent loop ($39.43 vs. $27.41), because the agentic hybrid retrieval is called inside the main loop and the agent spends additional turns issuing search queries. liu_refined moves the agentic exploration out of the main loop into refinement subagent that runs once per task before the main agent starts ($25.63), which drops the main-loop spend to $25.67 (below the no-skill baseline) but pushes the total to $51.30 for +9.0% lift over no skills. Takeaway. At marketplace scale, scaling within an open-source LM-based reranker family plateaus near 0.6 parameters and reaches observed parity with commercial-API rerankers and LLMmediated refinement; stage-1 recall, not stage-2 capacity, bounds the residual difference. The deterministic recipe records liu_refineds accuracy at much lower per-trial spend ($27.54 vs. $51.30), while keeping agent-side spend within fifty cents of the no-skill baseline and avoiding any in-loop LLM call. This positions the deterministic recipe as strong default under the SkillsBench tasks and OpenHands harness we tested, with LLM-mediated alternatives held in reserve for harder regimes.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SkillSeek, an open-source two-stage skill retriever (BGE-base bi-encoder feeding small cross-encoder, exposed over MCP) built from the standard IR recipe. Across the SkillsBench 89task benchmark, SkillSeek reaches observed parity with Liu et al. (2026b)s LLM-mediated loop at essentially no extra cost: plain BM25 alone suffices on three of four settings, and SkillSeek covers the remaining difference on the fourth, with pertrial spend dropping from $51.30 to $27.54. Under the SkillsBench tasks and OpenHands harness we tested, the standard IR recipe is strong default for agent-skill retrieval, with LLM-mediated alterna-

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We disclose the following limitations that frame how our results should be interpreted. Single-Trial Evaluation. Each main-grid setting is single 89-task trial. To estimate trial noise, we re-ran one setting (34K, MiniMax-M2.7, bgereranker-v2-m3) three times; the standard deviation was approximately 1%. We therefore treat differences below 2% as within noise, and rely on larger cross-pool effects (several percentage points) for the curated-vs-marketplace claim, not per-setting rankings. This is why we describe our central result as observed parity with Liu et al. (2026b)s loop: we report the pass rates each method achieved, and we claim no resolved advantage in either direction. Establishing equivalence in the stronger sense would require pre-specified practical margin and repeated independent rollouts of the headline Qwen3.5 settings, separating variation across tasks from variation across rollouts of the same task. We leave that replication to future work. Missing Trials Are Counted as Zero. trial that fails to complete, most often through an OpenRouter network error or timeout, contributes reward of 0 to the mean rather than being dropped. This convention lowers every methods absolute pass rate, and it applies identically to SkillSeek, to the classical baselines, and to Liu et al. (2026b)s loop, so it does not favor any method. It does compress the spread between methods, which makes the observed differences we report conservative in magnitude but not in sign. Backbone Noise on MiniMax-M2.7. On MiniMax-M2.7, OpenRouter network or timeout failures hit roughly half the 89 tasks per condition, dropping absolute pass rates by 5% to 10% and narrowing the gap between methods. We therefore treat Qwen3.5-397B-A17B as the headline backbone and use MiniMax-M2.7 only as supporting evidence. Selection Bias in the Curated 192-Pool. The 192-skill SkillsBench pool was hand-curated by Li et al. (2026) so that every task has relevant skill. Our small-pool numbers therefore reflect both retrieval quality and curator selection. We make no claim about the absolute 192-pool numbers; the main finding is the cross-pool pattern (lightweight rerankers suffice on the curated pool; heavier methods help on the marketplace pool). First-Stage Alternatives Are Compared by Recall Only. Our recall-ceiling analysis (4.4) compares first-stage retrievers by R@5, the fraction of tasks gold skills appearing in the top five candidates. Recall is cheap to measure because it needs no agent rollout, and it is the quantity our mechanism turns on, but it is not the quantity the papers conclusion is stated in. first-stage retriever with higher R@5 need not produce higher agent pass rate, since what matters downstream is whether the top-ranked skill is useful for the task, and our helpfulness-gap diagnostic (4.4) shows these two can move in opposite directions. Running the strongest first-stage alternatives through the same cross-encoder and the same agent loop would settle this, and we leave it to future work. Scope of the Claim. Every result here comes from the 89 SkillsBench tasks executed under one agent harness, OpenHands, with two backbones and two skill pools. We do not claim that the standard IR recipe is strong default for agent-skill retrieval in general, only that it is one under the tasks, harness, pools, and backbones we tested. Terminal, web, and software-engineering agents impose different retrieval demands, and whether the observed parity survives in those settings is open. Independently built skill-retrieval benchmarks such as SkillRet, which pairs 16,129 public agent skills with 4,392 evaluation queries (Kang et al., 2026), are the natural targets for testing whether the recipe transfers, and we leave that to future work.

sections.title: B Choice of Agent Harness
sections.content: Our retrieval conditions (bm25, rerank, liu_ hybrid, liu_refined) are exposed as MCP servers, so the harness must (i) speak MCP natively, (ii) be scriptable from Python with open-weight backbones, and (iii) be open-source so that harnessside optimizations cannot confound retrieval comparisons. Five candidate harnesses were available at the time of the experiments: Claude Code (Anthropic) is closed-source: its skill-discovery loop is unauditable. Codex CLI (OpenAI) is closed-source for the same reason and tied to single model family. Gemini CLI (Google) is open-source but ships only as Node.js subprocess over stdio with no Python SDK, and is tied to the Gemini family. Terminus-2 (used by SkillsBench evaluations and by Liu et al. (2026b) for Kimi K2.5) is deliberately-minimal benchmark baseline (approximately 1.5 LOC) with no native MCP and no skill module; SkillsBench added 11 skill loading via fork but MCP was never wired in. OpenHands SDK (All Hands AI) is openscriptable from source, model-agnostic, Python, and ships native MCP and skill modules. Of the five, only the OpenHands SDK combines an in-process Python agent loop with native MCP, which our driver depends on for per-turn event capture and direct mcp_config injection.

sections.title: C Harness and Implementation Details
sections.content: We drive the OpenHands SDK directly rather than through wrapping CLI, with skills served over Model Context Protocol (MCP). Each trial uses fresh DockerDevWorkspace container, the agent receives the SkillsBench task instruction plus small system-message suffix nudging it to call skill_lookup before exploring the workspace, and the run is capped at 30 agent turns and 600 seconds of wall-clock. The MCP server (skills_mcp.py) exposes three tools: skill_ lookup(query, k) returns the top-k candidates as name: description lines; skill_load(name) returns the full SKILL.md body for named skill; skill_list() returns every skill name and description (rarely used by the agent). serverside X-Skill-Method header lets the experimental driver swap which retriever skill_lookup runs without changing the agents tool schema, keeping all per-condition runs A/B-comparable. For the none, oracle, and all conditions of the workshop ablation we bulk-mount skills via the harnesss standard AgentContext.skills channel; for the retrieval conditions the agent calls skill_lookup on demand. Retrieval-Tool Invocation. In every retrievalenabled condition we inject two instruction fragments into the agents context. The first is appended to the system prompt: IMPORTANT: skill retrieval tool named skill_lookup is available. Before exploring the workspace or running commands, you MUST call skill_ lookup with short query summarizing the task to discover relevant domain skills. Then call skill_load on the most relevant result to read its full content. The second is appended to the first user message: [REQUIRED FIRST STEP] Your very first tool call must be skill_lookup with 5 to 15 word query that summarizes this task. Then call skill_load on the most relevant result. Only after at least one skill_load call may you start working on the task. Empirically the system-only nudge produced roughly 40% to 60% skill_lookup invocation across backbones; the dual nudge raised it to 95.5% on every tested backbone.

sections.title: D Baseline Reimplementation
sections.content: The main grid in 4.2 compares SkillSeek against Liu et al. (2026b)s two loops under identical conditions: same agent harness, same backbones, same task budget, same trial count. To enable this likefor-like comparison, we reimplement Liu et al. (2026b)s liu_hybrid and liu_refined inside our experimental driver, drawing on their opensourced code and prompts. This appendix documents the reimplementation and states which way its deviations cut. Every deviation reduces what our liu_refined can do relative to the published version, so the accuracy comparison favors SkillSeek: fully faithful reimplementation would raise liu_refineds pass rates and narrow or reverse the differences we report. This is one reason we state the headline result as observed parity and claim no advantage in either direction. The cost comparison runs the other way, and in our favor: the capabilities we dropped are open-ended exploration and unlimited refined-skill output, both of which would raise liu_refineds token spend above the $51.30 we measure. Retrieval Server. Our search_server matches Lius behavior: BM25 fused with Qwen3Embedding-4B via reciprocal-rank fusion at = 60, exposing the same /keyword, /semantic, /hybrid, and /detail endpoints. Two minor implementation choices differ from the published source: we use the rank_bm25 Python package (no stemming) instead of SQLite FTS5, and we omit the optional content-embedding blend in the hybrid endpoint. The agent-side discovery prompt is verbatim port of Lius published skill, redirected to our server port. Refinement Prompt. The refinement prompt we use is conservative subset of Lius published INSTRUCTION_PROMPT: skills are retrieved via 12 curl to our server (vs. pre-populated directory), exploration is capped at 10 commands (vs. openended), we drop the optional skill-creator metaskill, and we cap output at 1 to 3 refined skills (vs. unlimited). Each of these choices reduces what our liu_refined can do relative to the published version. On the 34K / Qwen3.5 cell, where Qwen3Reranker-0.6B and liu_refined both reach 0.442, fully faithful reimplementation could therefore lift liu_refined above our retriever, and readers should treat the observed parity on that cell as the optimistic reading for SkillSeek. Reproduction Gap. On the 192-pool Qwen3.5397B-A17B cell, Liu et al. (2026b) report that query-specific refinement lifts pass rate from 0.267 to 0.308 (+4.1%), whereas our measurement shows refinement hurting (0.470 to 0.397, -7.3% delta). This sign flip is consistent with Lius own data: on Kimi K2.5 they also report refinement hurting (0.335 to 0.267, -6.8%). Our prompts conservatism explains part of the residual gap on Qwen3.5; on the settings where we report parity, the direction of the published delta matches ours.

sections.title: Pool
sections.content: The numbers in Table 10 come from pilot sweep we ran prior to the main grid (4) with three conditions (no skills, the full 192-skill pool loaded into context, and the per-task curated subset of 1 to 3 skills) on the same 89 SkillsBench tasks. The agent backbone was gpt-oss-120b served locally via vLLM on the two-RTX-6000 stack described in Appendix L; the harness was the OpenHands SDK with skills served over MCP, identical to the main-grid setup. Each setting aggregates three trials per task (267 trials per condition). Token totals are agent-side spend on gpt-oss-120b for the full trial (system prompt, task instruction, agent turns, and tool responses), averaged across trials. We treat the pilot as supporting evidence rather than primary result. stronger backbone might absorb more of the noise from loading all 192 skills, but the directional finding holds: an exhaustive load is not viable substitute for selection. This is consistent with the main-grid evidence that even bm25 outperforms loading the full pool.

sections.title: E Backbone Strength
sections.content: G Tool-REX Profile Iteration The two open-weight backbones differ in capability and stability. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B sits at Code-Arena score 1,257; MiniMax-M2.7 sits at 1,158, an approximately 99-point gap that translates to an 8.5% gap on our none baseline (0.352 vs. 0.267). The capability ordering is consistent across both pools and four trial sessions. On the noise axis, the two are not comparable: MiniMax-M2.7 trials hit ConversationRunError, TimeoutError, or MaxIterationsReached on 48 to 57 of the 89 tasks per condition (a method-independent error rate of roughly 50% to 64%), whereas Qwen3.5397B-A17B trials see near-zero such failures. The mechanism is straightforward: stage-2 reranker that surfaces the most useful skill is irrelevant when the downstream agent cannot reliably execute on it. The method-level signal on MiniMax-M2.7 is therefore limited by how often the agent crashes, not by retrieval quality. For this reason we treat Qwen3.5-397B-A17B as the headline backbone and MiniMax-M2.7 as supporting evidence, adjudicated by the lift between conditions on MiniMaxM2.7 rather than by absolute scores. Tool-REX v3 is the third iteration of the prompt used to expand each skills index text with structured tags. We generated all three iterations offline with locally served gpt-oss-120b (vLLM); the index is computed once per pool and reused across all retrieval trials at zero in-loop LLM cost. We document the two earlier failures because they map cleanly to known failure modes of LLM-generated document expansion (Li et al., 2024). v1 (Freeform Tags): Surface-Form Drift. The first prompt asked the LLM for 3 to 5 freeform descriptive tags per skill. On pdf-excel-diff, this produced tags like file comparison, tabular data, document inspection but omitted the literal surface forms excel and xlsx. The crossencoder, which is sensitive to query-document surface overlap, then ranked the gold skill at position 2 or 3 instead of 1, dropping R@5 from 1.0 to 0.5 on this task and similar ones. v2 (File-Type + Libraries + Operations): Library-Name Hijack. The second prompt added explicit file-type and library-name tags, e.g., pdf pypdf reportlab pdfplumber. At marketplace scale this dominated the cross-encoder for any pdf-shaped query: the literal pdf skills Condition pass rate tokens/trial none (no skills loaded) all (entire 192-skill pool loaded) oracle (per-task curated subset, 13 skills) 0.384 0.387 0.484 268 426 (+59%) 314 (+17%) Table 10: Loading every skill from small pool already fails. On 89 SkillsBench tasks with locally served gpt-oss-120b backbone, loading the full 192-skill pool (all) yields the same pass rate as loading nothing (0.387 vs. 0.384) despite 59% token surcharge, while per-task curated subset (oracle) lifts pass rate to 0.484. tag list was dominated by Python library names rather than the term pdf itself, and library tags appeared on near-twin skills that were not the gold. court-form-filling dropped from R@5 = 1.0 to 0.0 at 34K scale. v3 (Final): Four Ordered Tags, No Library Names. The shipping prompt produces exactly four tags in fixed order: file-type, primary operation, two secondaries. No library-name tags. This is the version used as the indexing default in our main grid (4.2): on the 34K pool with MiniMaxM2.7 it lifts the agent pass rate by +12.8% over name+description baseline, with paired 24 wins, 5 losses, and 41 ties on the shared subset.

sections.title: H Ablation Details
sections.content: This appendix provides per-parameter mechanism analysis for the three sweeps in 4.3; the tables themselves (Tables 2, 3, 4) appear in the main text. Indexing Text Matters; Tool-REX Is the Right Deterministic Choice. Replacing the Tool-REX v3 index with plain name+description baseline drops pass rate by 2.2%, and appending raw body text drops it by further percentage point (-3.2%). The body-text loss is consistent with noise leakage: implementation detail in the body dilutes the discriminative name+description signal that the crossencoder relies on. The specific four-tag schema also matters: two earlier iterations of the Tool-REX prompt regressed on concrete tasks (a freeform-tag variant dropped R@5 on pdf-excel-diff from 1.0 to 0.5 by omitting the literal surface forms excel/xlsx; library-name-tag variant dropped court-form-filling from 1.0 to 0.0 at 34K scale by letting Python library names dominate the crossencoder). See Appendix for the full failure-mode analysis. Tool-REX v3 is the indexing default behind every SkillSeek entry in Table 1. Stage-1 Depth kinit = 20 Is the Best Choice; Deeper Hurts. naive reading of the recallceiling argument would predict that on the 34K pool, where stage-1 R@5 is far from saturated, deepening stage-1 should help the cross-encoder lift relevant skills. The data say otherwise. The reranker behaves best at kinit = 20; halving the depth costs 2.1%, and doubling or quintupling it costs 3.5 to 4.5%. The shape is consistent with the rank-1-commit framing of 4.4: when the agent loads only the rank-1 candidate, what matters is the cleanliness of the very top of the cross-encoder ranking, not raw recall depth. More candidates in the cross-encoders input set introduce more pairwise comparisons that can perturb the rank-1 choice. The Rank-1-Commit Framing Holds, with Few Backup Candidates. At the agent interface, = 1 costs 2.0% relative to = 5, while = 3, = 5, and = 10 are tied within 1%. The agent commits to rank-1 most of the time but does benefit from one or two backup candidates when the cross-encoders top-1 is wrong. Beyond = 5, additional candidates buy essentially nothing. Helpfulness-Gap Diagnostic: Sign

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.content: The formal definition of the helpfulness gap is given in 4.4. The sign of has three readings. positive means retrieving the gold helps the agent; near-zero means the retrieval signal is washed out by other factors (agent noise, execution difficulty); negative means the retrieved gold actively confuses the agent relative 0.025 in to miss. Voyage rerank-2.5s = Figure 2(b) is the clearest negative case in our data.

sections.title: J Risks
sections.content: Skill retrieval systems can amplify risks present in the underlying skill pool. SkillSeek surfaces whichever skills the index rates as most relevant; it does not audit, sandbox, or verify them. malicious or low-quality skill in the pool can be surfaced and then executed inside the agents loop; recent attacks demonstrate guidance-injection 14 via skill bootstrap hooks (Liu et al., 2026a) and abandoned-repository hijacks on public marketplaces (Holzbauer et al., 2026). SkillSeek inherits this exposure in full: poisoned skill in the pool will be ranked alongside legitimate ones. natural risk-aware extension would compose SkillSeeks retrieval with preload risk scorer (Hou and Yang, 2026) to drop highrisk candidates before they reach the agent. The retriever itself introduces no new attack surface beyond the underlying pool. It runs locally, makes no external network calls beyond the LLM provider the host harness already contacts, and exposes only three read-only MCP tools (skill_lookup, skill_load, skill_list); none of these write to the filesystem or modify agent state outside the standard MCP request-response channel. The retriever also does not persist user queries, agent state, or task content across runs.

sections.title: K Use of Existing Artifacts
sections.content: Our code is released at https://github.com/ guanqun-yang/SkillSeek. We use two existing artifacts to construct the evaluation grid in 4. The first is the SkillsBench task suite and skill pool of Li et al. (2026), distributed under the Apache-2.0 license.12 The second is the 34,000-skill marketplace pool of Liu et al. (2026b) (code13, dataset14), with no license file present at the time of access (2026-05-24). Neither artifact ships an explicit intended use statement. We use both as agent-skill retrieval benchmarks, consistent with the framing in the original papers. Statistics. SkillsBench contains 89 deterministically verifiable tasks paired with 233 SKILL.md files (approximately 2.6 skills per task) that deduplicate to 192 unique skill names; Li et al. (2026)s published Table 1 uses an 84-task subset that omits 5 tasks whose verifier was not yet deterministic at their snapshot date, and we evaluate on the full 89. The Skill-Usage marketplace pool of Liu et al. (2026b) contains approximately 34,000 skills harvested from public hubs and filtered by permissive licenses and content quality. Both pools are English-only. SkillSeek is not trained on either pool, so we use each pool as single evaluation set 12https://github.com/benchflow-ai/skillsbench 13https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/SkillUsage 14https://huggingface.co/datasets/ShiyuLab/Skill-Usage with no train/dev/test split. Documentation. SkillsBenchs 89 tasks span scientific computing (e.g., flood-risk-analysis, gravitational-wave-detection, earthquakephase-association), data processing (e.g., pdfexcel-diff, parallel-tfidf-search), and applied software (e.g., adaptive-cruise-control, court-form-filling); the per-task difficulty labels we use in Table 8 come from task.toml in each task directory, with 3 of 89 tasks unlabeled. The Skill-Usage 34K pool covers broader application surface drawn from public skill hubs; Liu et al. (2026b) document the harvesting and filtering procedure in their appendix. PII and Offensive-Content Audit. We manually audited random sample of 5 SkillsBench tasks and 50 marketplace skills for personally identifiable information and for offensive content; we found no significant issues in either dimension. The sample is small, and we make no population-level claim about either pool; we report the audit only as sanity check on subset we read.

sections.title: L Computational Experiments
sections.content: Model Sizes. The bi-encoder (BGE-base) has 110 parameters and produces 768-dim embeddings; the default cross-encoder (bge-reranker-v2m3) has 568 parameters. The reranker scaling sweep of 4.4 uses Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B, Qwen3Reranker-4B, and Qwen3-Reranker-8B, with parameter counts matching their names. The two agent backbones in the main grid are Qwen3.5397B-A17B (397 total, 17 active per token) and MiniMax-M2.7; both are queried through OpenRouter. The Tool-REX v3 index expansion was generated offline by gpt-oss-120b served via vLLM. All canonical model identifiers are listed in Table 9. Compute Budget and Infrastructure. local vLLM stack with two NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPUs serves the two locally hosted models in this paper: gpt-oss-120b for the Tool-REX v3 index expansion, and Qwen3-Embedding-4B as the embedding component of Liu et al. (2026b)s baseline retriever. The Tool-REX v3 index expansion required under 2 GPU-hours on this stack and is computed once per pool, then reused across all retrieval trials. At lookup time the bi-encoder and cross-encoder of SkillSeek run on CPU at approximately 1.1 median (1.9 at p95) per skill_lookup call (4.4); the BGE-base embedding of the 34K pool is built 15 once on the same workstation and reused thereafter. Agent rollouts run through OpenRouter; per-trial token cost is reported in Table 6, and per-backbone OpenRouter spend for the full set of experiments in this paper is broken down in Table 11. For the commercial-reranker sweep in 4.4 (Figure 2), Voyage AI provides 200 million free tokens per account for both rerank-2.5 and rerank2.5-lite.15 Our 89-task sweep did not exhaust this one-time allowance, so the prepaid $50 credit on the account was not drawn down. Backbone OpenRouter spend (USD) Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (primary) MiniMax-M2.7 (secondary) GLM 5 (exploratory) Kimi K2.6 (exploratory) Total 617.77 149.19 45.84 24.67 837.47 Table 11: OpenRouter API spend per backbone. Totals for the four LLM backbones queried during this work. The two locally served models (gpt-oss-120b for the Tool-REX v3 index expansion and Qwen3Embedding-4B for Liu et al. (2026b)s baseline retriever) ran on the two-GPU vLLM stack described above and are not on OpenRouter. Captured from the OpenRouter usage dashboard on 2026-05-24. Package Versions and Parameter Settings. The BM25 baseline uses rank_bm25 with default tokenization (no stemming and no FTS5-style filtering, as documented in Appendix D). The bi-encoder and cross-encoder are loaded through sentencetransformers at their HuggingFace defaults; we do not fine-tune. The retrieval interface uses the official mcp Python SDK, and the agent loop uses the OpenHands SDK with the harness configuration documented in Appendix C. The Tool-REX v3 prompt is served via vLLM with greedy decoding (temperature 0, max_tokens capped to 256 per skill); the full prompt is reproduced in Appendix G.

sections.title: M GenAI Disclosure
sections.content: We maintained complete human authorship over the intellectual core of this study. We used Claude Code to assist with typesetting tasks (such as building tables, diagrams, and plots) and LLMs to refine our wording, but no AI was used to conceptualize ideas, generate data, or perform evaluations. We designed all algorithms, wrote the experimental code, and drafted the manuscript entirely ourselves. 15https://docs.voyageai.com/docs/pricing
